**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and *left* and *right* always mean
the offense's left and right. On offense, C is the center (the other four linemen are unlettered), Q the
quarterback, R the running back, F the fullback, Y the tight end, and X, Z and H receivers. Defensive linemen are
labelled by their [technique number](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-technique-alignment-number) (5, 3, 1),
S, M and W are the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, $ is the nickel back, CB a cornerback, and FS and SS the free
and strong safeties. Blue lines ending in a short bar are blocks; orange arrows are where defenders go; the thick
dark-blue arrow is the ball carrier. In the frame strips, faint lines are where each player has been.

## What a run fit is

Start with the offense, because run defense only makes sense as an answer to it. Every run play in
[Part 3](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) is built around one of two ideas. Either it creates a
*crease* the defense did not expect (zone's moving wall and cutback), or it creates an *extra blocker* at one spot
(power's pulling guard, the fullback on an iso, the quarterback's read on the option). Both ideas attack the same
weakness: a defender who is not where his teammates think he is.

So the defense's first answer is not a technique or a tackle. It is a plan. A
[**run fit**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-run-fit) is the defense's plan for which defender takes which gap or
job against a run, and also the act of carrying it out: each defender getting to his gap after the snap, on the
correct side of whoever is blocking him. Coaches use the word both ways. "Our fits were bad" means people went to
the wrong places; "he fit it perfectly" means one player arrived in his gap at the right moment, on the right
shoulder.

The principle underneath every fit has a name of its own:
[**gap integrity**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-gap-integrity). Every gap the offense can run through has
exactly one defender responsible for it, and each defender stays in his gap until the ball shows him where it is
going. "Exactly one" cuts both ways. A gap with nobody in it is an obvious problem: that is where the long run
goes. A gap with *two* defenders in it is the same problem in disguise, because the defense only has so many
players. If two defenders are in the B gap, some other gap is empty, and a good running back will find it.

You met the counting in [Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd): against a formation with one
tight end there are seven gaps along the line (two A gaps either side of the center, two B gaps, two C gaps, and a D
gap outside the tight end), and a one-gap defense puts one defender in charge of each. That count was the static
version. Run fits are what happens when the count starts moving, and it moves for three reasons:

1. **Blockers carry gaps with them.** A gap is not a patch of grass; it is the space between two blockers. When the
   tight end blocks down on the man inside him, the C gap slides inward with him, and a new space opens outside.
2. **Backs add gaps.** A fullback who runs to the line, or a guard who pulls, is one more blocker at one spot, and the
   space beside him is one more gap. Coaches say *every back in the backfield can add a gap*. Power's whole point is to
   create a gap at the point of attack that the defense did not have a man for before the snap.
3. **The defense moves too.** Linemen slant, linebackers blitz, safeties rotate. Each of those moves takes a defender
   out of one gap and puts him in another, so somebody else has to inherit the gap he left.

A fit is the defense's way of keeping the count right *while* all of that happens. Before the snap, each defender
knows his gap. After it, each knows how his gap changes when he sees a particular block: if the tackle in front of me
blocks down, my gap is outside; if the guard pulls, the linebacker behind me fast-flows and I inherit his. The
names you will learn in this chapter (force, spill, box, alley) are the vocabulary of those changes.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
A defense has eleven players and the offense knows where the ball is going; the defense does not. Run fits exist so
that the defense does not need to know. If every gap has an owner and every owner knows how his gap moves when the
blocking changes, the ball can go anywhere and somebody is waiting. The price is discipline. A fit only works if all
eleven players do their job *instead of* chasing the ball, which means trusting the man next to you. The most
talented player on the field can wreck a defense by "making a play" outside his gap and leaving it empty.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden, the move every user learns is to grab the safety, wait for the handoff and sprint at the ball carrier. It
works because the computer plays the other ten defenders' gaps perfectly. In real football, a player who leaves his
gap to make a play is the most common reason for a long run, and coaches grade it as a missed assignment even when
he makes the tackle. When you see a 60-yard run on a broadcast, rewind to the snap and look for the defender who ran
to the wrong side of a block. It is rarely the man who missed the tackle at the end.
:::

## Force: who turns the ball back inside

Every run has an inside and an outside, and the outside is where the defense has fewest bodies. So before anyone
talks about gaps, the defense names one player on each side of the ball whose job is the outside edge. He is the
[**force defender**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-force-defender), or "the force": the defender responsible for
keeping the ball carrier from getting outside him on a run to his side and for turning (*forcing*) the ball back
inside, toward the teammates who are chasing it. He does not have to make the tackle. He has to make the runner
change direction, back into the crowd.

You have met two cousins of this idea. In [Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd), to
**set the edge** was a *technique*: the outermost defender on the line takes on a blocker with his outside arm free so
the run can't get outside him. **Contain** was a rule about the quarterback escaping the pocket or running a bootleg.
Force is a *role*. It belongs to whichever defender the call assigns, and the call changes from play to play. Sometimes
the force is the defensive end, setting the edge exactly as 05-01 drew it. Often it is an outside linebacker, a nickel
back or a safety a few yards outside the end. In some coverages it is a cornerback.

Why would a cornerback be the force? Because the coverage decides who is free. A defender who has a deep zone to
protect cannot also come up to the line to turn a run inside; a defender with a short zone, or with no zone at all,
can. That is why the first question to ask about a run defense is not "who's in the box?" but "what are the safeties
and corners doing?" Two common answers, which you will see drawn in full in the coverage chapters:

- **Safety force (Cover 3, "sky").** One safety plays the deep middle; the other comes down to the strong side,
  outside the tight end, and becomes the force. The corners are deep, so they cannot be. This is the eighth man in the
  box, the shape of [Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) and its sky rotation.
- **Corner force (Cover 2, "cloud").** Both safeties stay deep, splitting the field in halves. The corners have no
  deep zone, so they sit at about five yards, a step outside the widest receiver, and come up to force the run.
  This is the classic shape of [Cover 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd).

Who stands just *inside* the force is the next question, and it is the subject of the next section, but you can see
both answers at once in @fig-force-alley.

```{python}
#| label: fig-force-alley
#| fig-cap: "Force and alley depend on the coverage. Same power-side picture, run to the right. Left, Cover 3 'sky': the strong safety has come down outside the tight end and is the force (purple ring), coming up outside-in; the free safety comes down from the deep middle to fill the alley (green ring, green lane). Right, Cover 2 'cloud': both safeties stay deep, the cornerback squats at five yards and is the force, and the safety on that side fills the alley from his deep half. The man outside forces; the man inside him fills the alley."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6))
for ax, (ttl, dfn, force, alley, fnote, anote) in zip(axes, [
        ("Cover 3 (sky): safety force",
         over_front() + [D("SS", "SS", 6.5, 9.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS"),
                         D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 15.0, "CB")], "SS", "FS",
         "SS: force", "FS: alley"),
        ("Cover 2 (cloud): corner force",
         over_front() + [D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 9.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -9.0, "FS"),
                         D("RCB", "CB", 4.5, 15.8, "CB")], "RCB", "SS",
         "CB: force", "SS: alley")]):
    p = Play(i_form(), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.highlight(force, color=PURPLE); p.highlight(alley, color=GREEN)
    fp, ap = p.players[force], p.players[alley]
    go_to(p, force, (2.4, 11.4), "path", speed=4.5)
    go_to(p, alley, (5.0, 7.2), "path", speed=4.5)
    fl = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.0, 18.0), window=(-8.5, 15.5), title=False)
    lane(fl, p, 7.4, 13.2, -0.3, 6.0, color=GREEN, alpha=0.07)
    say(fl, p, 3.3, 11.4 if force == "SS" else 9.0, "the alley", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
    point_to(fl, p, (fp.d + (2.6 if force == "SS" else -3.4), fp.w + (3.0 if force == "SS" else -1.4)),
             (fp.d, fp.w), fnote, color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
    point_to(fl, p, (ap.d - 1.2, ap.w - 4.4 if alley == "FS" else ap.w - 6.0), (ap.d, ap.w), anote, color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
    subtitle(ax, ttl)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The force has a hard job, and the technique he uses is mostly patience. He comes up *outside-in*: he approaches the
ball from outside its path, keeping his inside shoulder toward the runner and his outside arm free, never letting
the runner's helmet get to his outside. Come up too fast and too far inside, and a back with any speed simply runs
around him, a "leaky" or "soft" edge. Come up too slowly, and the back turns upfield inside him for seven yards before
anyone arrives. A good force player is the defense's answer to two of the offense's most dangerous plays: the outside
run that wins the corner, and the bounce, which is a run that was designed to go inside and ends up outside. The
bounce is the force's specialty, and it is where the next idea comes in.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The defensive end is always responsible for the outside." Sometimes he is, and then he sets the edge. But in many
calls the end is told to do the opposite: take on blocks *inside* and let somebody else have the outside. Whether the
end is the force or not is decided by the call and the coverage, and you can often tell before the snap. If a safety or
a corner is standing five to seven yards deep just outside the tight end, the end probably isn't the force.
:::

## Spill or box: two ways to meet a kick-out

Now go back to the play this chapter opened with. Power's kick-out block, from [Gap and Power
Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd), asks a question of the end man on the line (here, the Sam
linebacker standing up outside the tight end): a fullback is coming at you from the inside, and a pulling guard and
the running back are right behind him. What do you do?

There are two answers, and every defense teaches both.

[**Spill**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spill). The defender attacks the blocker's *inside* half. He gets
his outside shoulder and arm across the blocker's body, under him, toward the hole, a move coaches call a
*wrong arm* (or wrong shoulder), because it uses the arm a defender is usually taught to keep free. He is not trying
to win. He is trying to make a pile in the hole: his body, the fullback's body, and soon the pulling guard, who arrives
to find his lane full of bodies. The running back, who was following that guard, has nowhere to go inside, so the ball
*spills* outside, sideways along the line.

[**Box technique**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box-technique), also called
[**squeeze**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-squeeze). The defender keeps his outside arm free, meets the blocker
with his inside shoulder, and drives him back inside, squeezing the hole from the outside so it gets smaller and
smaller. He is "boxing" the ball in: it cannot get outside him, so it has to stay inside, where the linebackers are
filling. (Don't confuse box *technique* with *the* box, the area near the ball where defenders are counted. The
words are unrelated; football just reuses them.)[^svec]

The two techniques send the ball to opposite places, and that is the whole point of choosing between them. A defender
who spills is promising that someone is waiting *outside*. A defender who boxes is promising that someone is waiting
*inside*. In @fig-spill-box the same power play meets both.

```{python}
#| label: fig-spill-box
#| fig-cap: "Spill or box: the same power play against two techniques by the end man (the Sam, ringed in orange; the running back is ringed in green). Top row, spill: the Sam attacks the fullback's inside half in the backfield, the pile fills the hole, and the ball bounces outside to the strong safety, the force, with the Mike flowing over the top. Bottom row, box: the Sam squeezes down with his outside arm free and takes the kick-out at the line, the hole shrinks to a yard, and the Mike fills it and meets the pulling guard. Each technique sends the ball to a different teammate."
def kick_play(call):
    """Power right with the play side only; call = 'spill' or 'box' for the end man (the Sam)."""
    off = [q for q in i_form(wrs=False)]
    dfn = over_front() + [D("SS", "SS", 6.5, 10.0, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.5, 4.3), via=[(-0.3, 4.75)])
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])
    go_to(p, "RG", (3.0, -1.2), via=[(0.05, 2.0)])
    go_to(p, "C", (0.35, -0.3), via=[(-0.45, -0.15)])
    go_to(p, "LT", (-1.9, -3.7), via=[(-1.0, -2.6)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.75)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, -1.8), "path", speed=3.0)
    if call == "spill":
        go_to(p, "SAM", (-1.0, 6.0), "path", speed=2.6)                     # attacks the F's inside half
        go_to(p, "FB", (-1.4, 6.8), via=[(-3.6, 5.0)], speed=6.5)           # meets him in the backfield
        go_to(p, "LG", (1.4, 5.0), "pull", speed=6.5,
              via=[(-1.5, -1.2), (-2.4, 0.4), (-2.3, 3.4), (-0.8, 4.6)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (1.8, 7.8), "path", speed=4.3, via=[(3.4, 3.6)])  # fast flow: over the top
        go_to(p, "RB", (2.0, 10.4), "run", speed=5.5, delay=0.2,
              via=[(-5.7, 1.2), (-3.4, 4.2), (-2.4, 7.8), (-0.2, 9.8)])
        go_to(p, "SS", (2.5, 11.2), "path", speed=2.6, via=[(4.4, 10.8)])
    else:
        go_to(p, "SAM", (0.4, 6.2), "path", speed=2.4)                      # squeezes down, outside arm free
        go_to(p, "FB", (-0.5, 5.4), via=[(-3.6, 5.0)], speed=6.5)           # kick-out meets him at the line
        go_to(p, "LG", (0.9, 4.8), "pull", speed=6.5,
              via=[(-1.5, -1.2), (-2.4, 0.4), (-2.3, 3.4), (-0.8, 4.6)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (1.9, 4.9), "path", speed=4.2, via=[(3.4, 3.6)])   # fills the hole, meets the puller
        go_to(p, "RB", (0.6, 4.2), "run", speed=5.5, delay=0.2, via=[(-5.7, 1.2), (-3.4, 4.2), (-1.4, 4.6)])
        go_to(p, "SS", (3.6, 9.4), "path", speed=2.2)                       # stays outside: nothing out here
    return p


SPILL, BOX = kick_play("spill"), kick_play("box")


animation_or_strip(
    [(SPILL, 0.0, "spill"), (SPILL, 1.2, "spill"), (SPILL, 2.85, "spill"),
     (BOX, 0.6, "box"), (BOX, 1.2, "box"), (BOX, 2.0, "box")],
    ["the S (end man) waits\nfor the kick-out",
     "SPILL: S wrong-arms the F,\npiling up the hole",
     "ball bounces outside,\nwhere the SS (force) meets it",
     "BOX: S squeezes down,\noutside arm free",
     "F kicks him at the line;\nthe hole shrinks",
     "ball stays inside, into\nthe M filling the hole"],
    lateral=(-3.0, 13.5), window=(-9.0, 8.5), ncols=3, width_in=6.5,
    rings=(("SAM", style.DEFENSE), ("RB", style.THIRD)))
```

Follow the end man, ringed in orange, through both rows. In the top row he spills: he attacks the fullback before
the fullback can get to him, takes him down in the backfield, and the pulling guard turns up into a lane already full
of bodies. The back has nowhere to go but out, and out is where the strong safety, the force, is waiting with the
Mike linebacker flowing over the top behind him. In the bottom row he boxes: he steps down, keeps his outside arm
free and lets the fullback hit him at the line of scrimmage. The hole the play designed is still there, but it is a
yard wide instead of three, and the Mike fills it downhill and meets the pulling guard right in it. The back has
nowhere to go but straight into the collision.

### Why choose one or the other?

Both techniques work. Both fail. The difference is *how* they fail, and a defense picks the failure it can live with.

**Spill sends the ball to speed.** A run that bounces sideways is running at the slowest angle in football: it gains
no yards while it moves, and every defender on the field can chase it. Defenses with fast linebackers and safeties
love to spill, because they would rather tackle a back in space with three pursuers than in a crowded hole with one.
Spill also attacks the heart of a gap scheme. Power and counter depend on the puller turning up into a clean hole;
take the hole away and the play's best blocker becomes a spectator. The risk is the outside. A spilled ball is going
exactly where the defense has fewest bodies, and if the force is late, blocked or out of position, the back is around
the corner with nobody between him and the end zone.

**Box keeps the ball in the crowd.** Boxing keeps everything inside, where the big bodies are, and it is simpler for
the defenders outside: the force can stay outside and wait, because nothing is supposed to get to him. The risk is
inside. A boxing end who gets driven off the ball (the kick-out does its job) leaves a hole wider than the one the play
designed, and if the linebacker filling it is a step late or gets caught by the puller, the back runs through the
middle of the defense untouched.

A common way to organize all this, though staffs differ, is a pattern coaches sometimes call *spill inside, force
outside*: the players closest to the ball, linemen and inside linebackers, spill anything coming at them, and the
outermost defender on each side boxes, so that every spilled ball runs into a man who keeps it from getting further
out. In the top row of @fig-spill-box, that is exactly the shape: the Sam spills, the strong safety boxes. The ball
gets squeezed between them. Other defenses ask their end to box and their linebackers to spill the puller, and some
change the call by formation or by opponent. What matters for you watching on Sunday is the promise each technique
makes. When the end man wrong-arms a blocker, look outside for the man who has to be there.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
The tell is the end man's first contact. If he *dives under* the kick-out block toward the ball, it is a spill, and
the run should bounce: watch for the force. If he stays square, outside arm free, and takes the block on his inside
shoulder, it is a box, and the run should stay inside: watch the linebackers fill. When a broadcast shows a power run
from the end-zone camera, the pile in the hole after a spill is impossible to miss.
:::

## The alley player

Spill a ball outside and it does not go straight to the force. It goes first into the space *between* the box and the
force, a lane a few yards wide just outside the last defender on the line. Coaches call that lane the *alley*, and the
defender responsible for it is the [**alley player**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-alley-player): the man who
fills the gap between the force player and the box, meeting a run that has bounced outside the box but not outside the
force.

Look back at @fig-force-alley. In the Cover 3 picture the strong safety is the force and the free safety, coming down
from the deep middle, is the alley player; in some calls it is the Mike linebacker, flowing over the top. In the Cover 2
picture the cornerback is the force and the safety on that side is the alley player, coming down from his deep half.
In quarters ([Quarters and Match](../06-pass-coverage/06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd)), the two-high coverage that has
grown fastest in today's NFL,[^quarters] the outside linebacker or nickel back is usually the force and the safety is the alley player, who
reads the tight end and fills downhill the moment he sees him block. Names and exact assignments differ by staff, and
some defenses describe the same jobs with different words ("fold," "stack," "vice," "secondary contain").[^fitwords]
The geometry does not differ. Every sound fit has, on each side of the ball, an outside man who forces and a man inside
him who fills the alley.

Why does the alley player usually come from the secondary? Because he has to come from *outside the blocks*. The
linebackers start in the box, where blockers can reach them: a pulling guard leads up on the Mike, a tight end climbs
to the Will. A safety eight or twelve yards deep starts where no lineman can get to him before he reads the play.
That is also what he costs. A safety filling the alley is not covering the deep zone he started in. Play-action, which
[Play-Action, Boots and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) builds on exactly this,
is the offense's way of sending a receiver into the space the alley player just left.

## The fit chart: eleven defenders against power

Now put the pieces together for one play. Here is the same power play, right, against a 4-3 Over with a single-high
safety, the strong safety down outside the tight end, and the end man (the Sam) told to spill. A coach would draw this
as a **fit chart**: the play, with every defender's job written next to him. @fig-fit-chart is the picture and the table
under it is the chart. Read the table with the picture, one number at a time.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fit-chart
#| fig-cap: "An eleven-man fit chart against power right (the play of Gap and Power Runs), against a 4-3 Over with a single-high safety and the strong safety down. Blue: the blocks, the pulling guard and the running back's path. Orange arrows: where the defenders who move go. Rings: the spill player (orange), the force (purple) and the alley player (green). The numbers match the table below; every defender, including both cornerbacks, has a job."
def power_blocks(p):
    """Power right, as drawn in Gap and Power Runs: down blocks by the Y and the RT (the RG helps on the 3,
    then climbs to the Will), the C blocks back, the LT hinges, the LG pulls, the F kicks out the end man."""
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.5, 4.3), via=[(-0.3, 4.75)])
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.8), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])
    go_to(p, "RG", (3.4, -1.0), via=[(0.05, 2.0)])
    go_to(p, "C", (0.35, -0.3), via=[(-0.45, -0.15)])
    go_to(p, "LT", (-1.9, -3.7), via=[(-1.0, -2.6)])
    go_to(p, "LG", (2.5, 4.6), "pull", via=[(-1.7, -1.3), (-3.4, 0.2), (-3.4, 3.4), (-1.6, 4.9)])
    go_to(p, "FB", (-0.6, 6.2), via=[(-3.6, 4.8)], speed=5.0)
    return p


def badge(fld, p, d, w, n, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK):
    """A numbered tag that ties a defender to a row of the fit-chart table."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), str(n), fontsize=6.6, color="white", fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center",
                zorder=13, bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.18", fc=color, ec="white", lw=0.6))


# (defender, offset in d, offset in w) for the numbered tags, in the order of the fit-chart table
FIT_BADGES = [("WE", 0.0, -1.7), ("NT", 1.5, -0.9), ("DT", 1.5, -0.3), ("SE", 1.6, 0.5), ("SAM", 1.4, 1.3),
              ("MIKE", 1.4, 0.0), ("WILL", 0.0, -1.7), ("SS", 0.0, 1.8), ("FS", 0.0, -1.9), ("RCB", 0.0, 1.8),
              ("LCB", 0.0, 1.8)]


def sky_defense():
    """4-3 Over, single-high (Cover 3 'sky'): the strong safety down outside the Sam, the free safety in the
    deep middle, the corners deep."""
    return over_front() + [D("SS", "SS", 6.5, 9.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS"),
                           D("LCB", "CB", 7.5, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 15.0, "CB")]


p = Play(i_form(), sky_defense(), los=35, to_go=None, title="An 11-man fit chart: power right vs a 4-3 Over, Cover 3")
power_blocks(p)
go_to(p, "RB", (2.4, 9.3), "run", via=[(-5.7, 1.2), (-3.2, 4.4), (-1.6, 7.0)])
# the defense's fits (orange arrows): where each man goes to own his piece of the field
go_to(p, "SAM", (-0.4, 6.0), "path", speed=4.0)           # spill: wrong-arm the fullback
go_to(p, "SS", (2.9, 9.6), "path", speed=4.5)             # force
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.6, 6.4), "path", speed=4.5)           # fast flow outside, over the top of the pile
go_to(p, "WILL", (3.4, -0.4), "path", speed=3.0)          # slow flow: backside A gap, the cutback
go_to(p, "FS", (8.0, 6.0), "path", speed=4.5)             # alley, inside-out
go_to(p, "WE", (-1.6, -2.6), "path", speed=4.0)           # chase flat, check the bootleg
p.highlight("SAM", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("SS", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("FS", color=GREEN)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-18.0, 18.5), window=(-9.0, 16.0))
for n, (key, dd, dw) in enumerate(FIT_BADGES, start=1):
    q = p.players[key]
    badge(f, p, q.d + dd, q.w + dw, n)
say(f, p, -6.6, -11.0, "numbers: see the fit chart\nin the table below", fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```

| # | Defender | Job against power right | Why it matters |
|:-|:------|:-------------|:-----------|
| 1 | Backside end (5-technique, left) | Unblocked. Squeeze down the line, flat, and chase; check the quarterback for a bootleg or keeper first. | Power leaves him free on purpose. He is too far away to stop the play, so his job is the cutback, the boot and the reverse. |
| 2 | Nose (1-technique, left) | Hold the backside A gap against the center's back block. | If he gets pushed out of it, the cutback has a lane right up the middle. |
| 3 | Defensive tackle (3-technique, right) | Anchor against the double team in the B gap: give no ground, keep both blockers busy. | Every second he holds two blockers is a second the right guard can't climb to the Will. |
| 4 | Play-side end (5-technique, right) | Fight the tight end's down block, squeeze the C gap, stay on the blocker's outside hip. | If he is washed inside, the hole doubles in size. |
| 5 | Sam (end man, right) | **Spill**: wrong-arm the fullback's kick-out, as deep in the backfield as he can. | The pile he makes is the wall that sends the ball outside. |
| 6 | Mike | Fast flow: run over the top of the pile, outside, ready for the bounce. | He is the second man in the alley. If the puller catches him, the safety has to be right. |
| 7 | Will | Slow flow: shuffle, own the backside A gap and the cutback, then pursue from behind. | The right guard's climb is aimed at him. If he over-runs the play, the cutback is open. |
| 8 | Strong safety | **Force**: come down outside-in, keep the ball inside him, turn the bounce back. | The spill only works because he is there. |
| 9 | Free safety | **Alley**: come down from the deep middle, inside-out, into the lane between the pile and the force. | Third man to the ball, and the last one between a bounce and a long run. |
| 10 | Right cornerback | Deep third. Read the receiver in front of him; if the Z blocks *in* on the safety (a [crack block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-block)), he replaces the safety as the force. | The crack-and-replace rule keeps the edge from going empty when the offense blocks the force. |
| 11 | Left cornerback | Deep third on the backside: no deep pass behind him, then the last defender on any cutback that breaks. | Somebody has to stay home on a play-action pass. |

This is a typical way to fit the play, not one team's playbook: defenses vary the spill and box calls, who flows where,
and which safety comes down.

Three things are worth noticing.

**Everybody has a job, including the players far from the ball.** The left cornerback is fifteen yards from the play
and still has an assignment, and if he leaves it to chase the run, a play-action pass to the X receiver is a touchdown.
Fits are eleven-man plans, which is why defensive coaches say a run defense is only as good as its worst fit.

**The defense counts, and so does the offense.** Power brought seven blockers to the party (five linemen, the tight end
and the fullback). The defense brought eight defenders into and around the box (four linemen, three linebackers and the
strong safety), plus a free safety who can arrive late. That eighth defender is the subject of the next section, but
look where the defense spends him: as the force, *outside* the play, exactly where a spilled ball ends up. The fit
chart and the box count are the same idea seen from two sides.

**Gaps move, and the fits move with them.** Before the snap, the Mike was over the right A gap. After the snap, the
right A gap has a nose, a tackle and two linemen in it, and the Mike's job is outside the pile, three gaps over. He did
not freelance. He read his key, saw power, and went where the plan said power's gap would appear. Every linebacker's
read in [Linebackers and the Second Level](05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd) is a question about where his gap
has gone.

## Fits against zone: when the gaps keep moving

Power tells the defense where it is going. A pulling guard is a signpost, and a defense that reads it can fit the gap
the play creates. Zone does the opposite. As [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) showed, the
whole line steps the same way and the running back picks the hole *after* the snap, so there is no single gap to fit.
The gaps slide sideways with the blockers, and the back is reading the defenders to see which one is out of place.

Against zone, then, a fit is less a spot than a relationship: *stay on the correct side of your blocker, and stay a
gap behind the ball*. @fig-zone-fit draws it against outside zone.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-fit
#| fig-cap: "Fitting outside zone right. The line steps right and the back aims wide, so the gaps slide with the blockers. The play-side end stretches with the reach and keeps his outside arm free; the Sam is the force (purple ring), coming up outside-in; the Mike flows fast but stays a gap behind the ball; the Will slow-flows and owns the cutback (green ring), with the backside safety behind him in the cutback alley; the backside end squeezes, chases and watches for the bootleg."
off = line() + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
dfn = even4(sam_w=6.6) + [D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 11.0, -8.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None, title="Fitting outside zone: the gaps move, so the fits move")
for k, dw in [("LT", (0.0, 1.6)), ("LG", (0.0, 1.7)), ("C", (0.0, 1.7)), ("RG", (0.2, 1.8)), ("RT", (0.2, 1.9)),
              ("Y", (0.2, 2.2))]:
    p.block(k, pts=[dw])
go_to(p, "RB", (-1.5, 7.2), "run", via=[(-6.0, 2.6), (-3.6, 5.6)])
go_to(p, "SE", (0.8, 8.4), "path", speed=3.0)        # play-side end: step with the reach, outside arm free
go_to(p, "DT", (0.9, 4.6), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "NT", (0.9, 2.1), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "SAM", (3.0, 10.5), "path", speed=4.5)      # force: outside-in
go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.0, 4.6), "path", speed=4.5)      # fast flow, stay behind the ball
go_to(p, "WILL", (3.4, 0.2), "path", speed=2.5)      # slow flow: the cutback
go_to(p, "WE", (-0.6, -1.8), "path", speed=3.5)      # backside end: squeeze and chase
go_to(p, "SS", (7.0, 10.2), "path", speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "FS", (7.4, -1.0), "path", speed=4.0)       # backside safety: cutback alley
p.highlight("WILL", color=GREEN); p.highlight("SAM", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, width_in=5.9, lateral=(-12.0, 15.5), window=(-8.5, 13.5))
point_to(f, p, (-3.6, 12.2), (0.9, 8.4), "end: stretch with the\nreach, outside arm free", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (6.3, 13.4), (3.0, 10.5), "S: force,\noutside-in", color=PURPLE, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (7.6, 2.6), (3.6, 3.4), "M: fast flow, a gap\nbehind the ball", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (2.4, -8.2), (4.4, -2.0), "W: slow flow,\nown the cutback", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (8.4, -8.6), (9.4, -4.9), "FS: cutback\nalley", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
point_to(f, p, (-4.0, -5.0), (-0.6, -1.8), "end: squeeze,\nchase, boot", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

- **The play-side edge doesn't spill.** There is no kick-out to spill. The tight end or tackle is trying to *reach*
  the end man, get his head outside and seal him in. So the end man stretches with the reach, keeps his outside arm
  free and makes the ball cut up inside him. The Sam outside him is the force, coming up outside-in to stop the back
  from winning the corner. Together they squeeze the run back toward the middle, where the outside zone runner does not
  want to be.
- **The play-side linebacker runs, but behind the ball.** Fast flow, but never ahead of the running back's helmet. A
  linebacker who over-runs the play (gets outside the ball) has given the back a lane behind him, and zone is designed
  to find exactly that lane.
- **The backside owns the cutback.** This is where zone hurts defenses. Outside zone's biggest runs are cutbacks, so the
  backside linebacker slow-flows (shuffles, waiting) and owns the cutback lane, and the backside safety comes down into
  the alley behind him. The backside end squeezes down the line, chasing from behind, but with one eye on the
  quarterback: outside zone's best friend is the bootleg the other way.

Zone also explains the most common *failure* of gap integrity on a broadcast. When a zone run gets eight yards on a
cutback, rewind and look at the backside linebacker. Usually he flowed with everyone else, two defenders ended up in the
same play-side gap, and the backside gap he owned was empty. The back didn't make the hole. The defense gave it to him.

## The plus-one: where the extra defender comes from

So far this chapter has assumed something it hasn't said out loud: the defense has enough players to own every gap
and still have someone left over. Where does that someone come from?

[The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) introduced
[hat math](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hat-math-numbers-advantage): count the offense's blockers, count the box,
and compare. [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) turned it into
a scale (light, normal, loaded). The defensive side of that arithmetic has a name. The
[**plus-one**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-plus-one) is having one more run defender than the offense has
blockers, so one defender is unblocked and free to make the tackle. With six blockers, it means seven run defenders;
with seven, eight.

Why one *more*? Because if the numbers are even, every defender can be blocked. A hat on every hat means the
runner reaches the second level untouched unless some defender beats his blocker, and the defense would be betting its
whole run defense on winning one-on-one fights. With a plus-one, the defense doesn't need to win a single block. It
needs every defender to hold his gap, and the extra man makes the tackle. Look at the fit chart again: the strong
safety is the plus-one, and his job, force, is the one nobody on the offense was assigned to block.

The plus-one almost always comes from the secondary, because that is where the spare players are. The defense starts
with eleven; the corners are usually busy with the wide receivers, and one deep safety stays back to prevent the long
pass. Everyone else can be a run defender. So the cleanest way to add a defender to the box is to bring a safety down,
and the cleverest way is to bring him down *at the snap*, after the quarterback has looked at the defense.

```{python}
#| label: fig-plus-one
#| fig-cap: "The plus-one. Before the snap the defense shows two high safeties and six defenders in the box (shaded) against six blockers: a light box. At the snap the strong safety rotates down (arrow) to the spot ringed in purple, just outside the tight end, and the free safety rotates to the deep middle. The box is now seven against six, with one defender nobody is assigned to block."
off = single_back_11()
dfn = even4() + [D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.5, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None, title="The plus-one: a safety rotates into the box at the snap")
go_to(p, "SS", (5.8, 7.0), "path", speed=5.0)
go_to(p, "FS", (13.5, 0.0), "path", speed=5.0)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-8.0, 16.0))
lane(f, p, -5.4, 6.9, -0.6, 7.0, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.05)
spot_ss = p.players["SS"]
x, y = _P(f, p, 5.8, 7.0)
f.ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((float(x), float(y)), 4, radius=0.94, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT,
                              ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, zorder=8))
f.ax.text(float(x), float(y), "SS", fontsize=6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center", zorder=10)
f.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.45, fc="none", ec=PURPLE, lw=2.0, zorder=7))
say(f, p, -4.2, 11.0, "blockers: 6\n(5 linemen + Y)", fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 9.6, -12.0, "before the snap:\n6 in the box v 6 blockers", fontsize=6.8)
say(f, p, 3.0, 11.8, "after the rotation:\n7 v 6, the plus-one", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (10.4, -3.6), (13.3, -2.0), "FS rotates to the\ndeep middle", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

In @fig-plus-one the defense shows two high safeties before the snap. Count the box: four linemen and two
linebackers, six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end). That is a
[light box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box), and a quarterback with the freedom to check to a run at the
line would be tempted. At the snap, the strong safety rotates down into the box and the free safety slides to the deep
middle. Now it is seven against six, the plus-one, and the shell has turned from two-high into one-high. How the
defense hides that move until the last moment, and the names for the many ways to do it (a *sky* rotation, a *spin*
on motion), are the subjects of [Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) and
[Disguise and Rotation](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).

### The offense's answers, and the defense's answers to those

The plus-one is not a fixed fact. It is the opening position in a negotiation, and each side has a short list of moves.

**The offense can add a blocker.** A second tight end or a fullback makes seven blockers, so the defense needs eight
to stay plus-one. That is why heavy personnel is a run-game tool, and why it came back: in 2025 NFL offenses used fewer
than three wide receivers on 41.7% of plays, the first season at or above 38% since Next Gen Stats began tracking in
2016.[^heavy]

**The offense can spread the defense out.** Every receiver split wide pulls a defender with him. Four wide receivers
leave the defense with fewer players to put in the box at all.

**The offense can read the free man instead of blocking him.** This is the option idea from
[Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd), and it is the plus-one's natural enemy. If the
quarterback reads the unblocked defender and keeps the ball whenever that defender chases the back, the offense has
"blocked" him without spending a blocker, and the count is even again. So the rule of box math with a running
quarterback is simple: **count the quarterback as a blocker**. Six blockers plus a quarterback who reads is seven.

**The offense can throw.** Every safety in the box is a safety not covering a deep zone. The run-pass option
([RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd)) and play-action both turn the plus-one into a target.

And the defense's answers? It can bring yet another safety, and play with no deep safety at all, a gamble you will
meet in [Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd). It can change the *technique* instead
of the numbers: two-gapping linemen who each control two gaps let six defenders cover seven gaps, which is the whole
idea behind the tite front of [Odd and Hybrid Fronts](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd). Or it can accept the light box
and fit the run from depth, which is the next section, and the biggest strategic argument in the NFL right now.

## Fitting the option: the gap exchange

The zone read is plus-one arithmetic with a quarterback in it. [Option
Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) showed the offense's view: block everyone but the backside
end, read him, and hand the ball to whichever runner he is not taking. The defense's fit chart has to say who takes the
running back and who takes the quarterback, and the simplest version says the end takes the quarterback (he stays
home) and the linebacker behind him takes the inside gap. The offense knows that chart, so the end's behaviour tells
the quarterback what to do.

The defense's answer is to change the chart after the snap. A
[**gap exchange**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-gap-exchange) is a planned swap of gap responsibilities between two
defenders after the snap: one takes the other's gap and vice versa. The best-known version is the
[scrape exchange](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scrape-exchange) from 03-04: the end crashes inside at the running
back, which is the "keep" read, and the linebacker behind him scrapes over the top to take the quarterback.
@fig-exchange runs it as a fit. The tags show what each defender owns, before the snap and after it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-exchange
#| fig-cap: "The scrape exchange as a run fit (simulated). The line zones right and the quarterback reads the backside end. The tags show who owns what: before the snap the end has the quarterback and the Will (ringed in orange) the inside gap; at the snap they swap. The end crashes on the back, the quarterback (ringed in green) sees 'keep' and pulls the ball, and the Will, scraping over the top, meets him. The left guard climbs to where the Will used to be and finds nobody."
off = line() + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R")]
dfn = even4() + [D("SAM", "SAM", 4.4, 6.4, "S")]
ZR = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, end in [("LT", (0.4, -2.6)), ("C", (0.4, 0.5)), ("RG", (0.4, 2.6)), ("RT", (0.5, 4.2)), ("Y", (0.6, 6.0))]:
    go_to(ZR, k, end)
go_to(ZR, "LG", (3.4, -2.0), via=[(-0.3, -1.4), (1.0, -1.8)])     # climbs to where the Will was
go_to(ZR, "WE", (-2.4, -2.0), "path", speed=4.0)                  # the end crashes on the back
go_to(ZR, "WILL", (-0.6, -6.6), "path", speed=5.6, via=[(3.6, -4.8), (1.4, -6.4)])   # scrapes over the top
go_to(ZR, "RB", (1.2, 2.4), "path", via=[(-4.7, -0.4), (-3.4, 1.0)])          # the fake
go_to(ZR, "QB", (0.6, -7.6), "run", delay=0.6, via=[(-4.6, -1.0), (-2.6, -4.6)])
go_to(ZR, "MIKE", (3.4, 2.6), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(ZR, "SAM", (3.0, 6.8), "path", speed=2.5)


def exchange_tags(fld, play, t, i):
    e, w = play.position("WE", t), play.position("WILL", t)
    if t < 0.3:
        gap_tag(fld, play, -2.6, -7.0, "E: the QB", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
        gap_tag(fld, play, 6.6, -2.6, "W: inside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4)
    else:
        gap_tag(fld, play, -6.2, e[1] + 1.6, "E: the back", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.4)
        gap_tag(fld, play, w[0] + 2.0, max(w[1] + 1.2, -8.6), "W: the QB", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.4)
    if t >= 1.7:
        spot(fld, play, 0.3, -7.4)


animation_or_strip(
    [(ZR, 0.0, ""), (ZR, 0.6, ""), (ZR, 1.1, ""), (ZR, 1.8, "")],
    ["the plan the Q expects:\nthe end has the QB",
     "the end crashes: the read\nsays 'keep'",
     "the Q pulls it; the Will is\nalready scraping outside",
     "the Will meets the Q;\nthe LG climbed to nobody"],
    lateral=(-11.5, 8.5), window=(-7.5, 8.5), ncols=2, width_in=5.6,
    rings=(("WILL", style.DEFENSE), ("QB", style.THIRD)), after=exchange_tags)
```

The quarterback did everything right. He read the end, the end took the back, and he kept the ball. The defense
simply moved the man who owned the quarterback, and it did it after the quarterback's eyes had stopped looking for
him. Notice the cost, too, in the last frame: the left guard climbed to the spot where the Will used to be and found
nobody. The Will's original gap, the backside B gap, was empty for a moment. If the back had kept the ball (if the end
had stayed home after all, or the quarterback had handed off), that gap would have been the hole. A gap exchange is a
bet that the offense will read the *first* picture.

Gap exchanges are not only for the option. A defensive line [slant](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant-line-movement)
(05-01) is a gap exchange for a whole front: every lineman moves over one gap and the linebackers move the other way
to fill what they left. An end who "spikes" inside while the outside linebacker takes his C gap is one; so is a
linebacker who blitzes through the A gap while the nose loops into the B gap. The idea is always the same: keep gap
integrity (every gap still has exactly one owner) while changing *which* defender owns it, so the blocking scheme
and the quarterback's read, both built on the pre-snap picture, are wrong. That is also the logic of the
[simulated pressures](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd) of Part 7, applied to the pass game.

Against a team built on the option, defenses also rewrite the chart in option language. Instead of gaps, a coach
assigns *dive* (the running back on the inside run), *quarterback* and, if there is one, *pitch*, and he makes sure
each has an owner on every play, with the assignments rotating between players from snap to snap so the quarterback
never sees the same picture twice. That is the logic you will see from the defensive side of
[The Ravens' Option Run Game](../12-case-studies/12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game.qmd).

## Two-high and the light box: inviting the run on purpose

Everything so far says the defense wants a plus-one in the box. For most of football history, that was the end of the
discussion. Then, starting in the late 2010s, more and more NFL defenses began doing something that looked backward:
keeping both safeties deep, playing six (sometimes five) defenders in the box against six blockers, and daring the
offense to run.

Here is the shape of it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-light-box
#| fig-cap: "The two-high light box against inside zone. Six blockers, six defenders in the box: the guards climb to the linebackers and every defender has a blocker. The defense's free men are the two safeties (purple rings), filling from 12 yards. By the time they arrive, the run has reached the shaded area, four or five yards downfield: the yards the defense has agreed to give."
off = single_back_11()
dfn = [D("WE", "DL", 1.0, T("5", -1), "5"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, T("1", -1), "1"),
       D("DT", "DL", 1.0, T("3", 1), "3"), D("SE", "DL", 1.0, T("5", 1) + 1.6, "5"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.8, 1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.8, -2.4, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.5, "$"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "CB"),
       D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.5, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None, title="Two-high, light box: the plus-one comes from 12 yards away")
for k, end in [("LT", (0.4, -4.0)), ("LG", (3.6, -2.3)), ("C", (0.4, -0.6)), ("RG", (3.6, 1.0)),
               ("RT", (0.4, 2.4)), ("Y", (0.4, 5.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
go_to(p, "RB", (5.0, 2.6), "run", via=[(-5.2, 0.6), (-1.0, 1.9)])
go_to(p, "SS", (5.6, 3.4), "path", speed=6.0)
go_to(p, "FS", (7.2, -0.6), "path", speed=6.0)
p.highlight("SS", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("FS", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-17.0, 17.0), window=(-8.0, 15.5))
lane(f, p, -2.2, 6.6, 0.0, 4.6, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.08)
say(f, p, 2.6, -9.0, "6 v 6: a hat on every hat;\nnobody in the box is free", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (2.6, 10.6), (4.6, 2.9), "the run gets here\nbefore a safety arrives:\n4 to 5 yards", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (9.6, 1.0), (8.6, 4.9), "safeties fill from depth:\nthe plus-one, late", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```

In @fig-light-box the box is even: six defenders, six blockers, a hat on every hat. Nobody in the box is free. The
plus-one still exists, but it is twelve yards away: the two safeties, who read run and come downhill as alley players.
They are the defense's free men, and they arrive late, somewhere around four or five yards downfield. The defense has
done the box math and decided to pay a few yards on every run in exchange for something it values more.

### Why a defense would do this

**Explosive passes cost more than runs.** [Expected Points and Success
Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd) showed that the average pass gains more
than the average run, and the big losses for a defense are explosive pass plays. Two deep safeties are the best
protection against them. A defense that keeps two high is choosing to give up four-yard runs rather than forty-yard
passes. You will see in the data below that this is a sensible trade.

**Two-high shells can disguise.** A defense that shows two safeties can still rotate into one-high at the snap (the
plus-one of @fig-plus-one) or play any of the two-high coverages behind it. The light box keeps the offense guessing
about who will be in it a second after the snap.

**It has been spreading.** Next Gen Stats measured split-safety coverage on 32.9% of plays in 2018, 40.4% in 2024 and
42.0% in 2025, the highest since its tracking began.[^twohigh] The box counts moved with it: in the nflverse data,
designed runs met six or fewer defenders in the box about 38% of the time in 2018–2022, and 58% and 55% of the time in
2024 and 2025.[^lightshare]

The coach most associated with the approach is **Vic Fangio**, an NFL assistant for more than thirty years before
Denver made him a first-time head coach at 60 (2019–2021), whose two-high defenses in Chicago and Denver spread across the
league, carried first by coaches who had worked for him, such as Brandon Staley.[^fangio] His approach is simple to state: keep two safeties deep to take away
the explosive pass, and ask the front to hold the run without help. His linemen are asked to win their own fights and,
at times, to "steal" back gaps the box does not have bodies for, as a Philadelphia beat writer put it in 2024.[^inq] How
the counterrevolution started, and the answer to it, are history for
[The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd) and a case study,
[Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd).

### What it costs

The light box is a trade, and the bill comes in four parts.

- **Yards.** Runs against six-man boxes average more than runs against seven or eight: on early downs in the data
  below, about a quarter of a yard more per carry than against seven and more than half a yard more than against
  eight or more. A defense that lives in light boxes will look
  bad in rushing yards allowed, and it has accepted that.
- **The front must be good enough to hold.** A six-man box has no margin. If one lineman is moved off his gap, there is
  no spare linebacker behind him; the next defender is a safety at twelve yards. Light-box defenses need linemen who
  can take on double teams and two-gap when they have to, which is why they pay for big interior players and why the
  tite front of [Odd and Hybrid Fronts](05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd) became their favourite shape.
- **The safeties must tackle.** A safety fitting from depth meets the runner at full speed, in space, often one-on-one.
  A missed tackle there is not a four-yard run. It is a forty-yard run, because there is nobody behind him.
- **Heavy personnel attacks it.** Against a light box, the offense's simplest move is to add blockers, and the rise of
  two- and three-tight-end sets in 2024 and 2025 is partly that. Each extra blocker forces the defense to choose again:
  match it with a heavier package (base defense was on the field for 29.7% of snaps in 2025, up from a low of
  20.5% in 2023) or accept being outnumbered in the box.[^heavy2]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A light box means the defense is soft against the run." The 2024 Eagles faced runs with six or fewer defenders in the
box about two thirds of the time, among the three highest rates in the league, and allowed the fewest expected points
per designed run of any defense, by this book's count.[^fangiocalc] A light box is not the absence of a run fit. It is
a fit that uses the safeties instead of an eighth man at the line, and that asks more of the defensive line.
:::

## What the data says: box count and EPA

You can test all of this with the nflverse data. The participation files record how many defenders were in the box at
the snap on almost every play, and the play-by-play records the result. @fig-box-epa compares designed runs and
dropbacks by box count, on first and second down in neutral situations (so that third-and-long and the goal line,
where box counts and outcomes are both extreme, don't tilt the picture), for two eras of the data that count the box
in slightly different ways.

```{python}
#| label: fig-box-epa
#| fig-cap: "EPA per play by the number of defenders in the box at the snap, regular seasons 2018–2025, first and second down, win probability 20–80%, outside the last two minutes of each half and outside the opponent's 10-yard line. Left: designed runs (quarterback scrambles excluded). Right: dropbacks (passes, sacks and scrambles). Each extra defender in the box costs runs about 0.02 to 0.05 expected points and is worth about the same to the passing game, the box as a budget. Even against the lightest boxes, runs average less than dropbacks do against the heaviest. The two lines are the two data sources (NGS for 2018–2022, FTN for 2023–2025), which count the box slightly differently; bars are 95% intervals. Data: nflverse play-by-play and participation via nflreadpy."
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

style.apply()
frames = []
for yr in range(2018, 2026):
    part = nfl().load_participation([yr]).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "defenders_in_box"]]
    pb = pbp(yr, columns=["game_id", "play_id", "season_type", "play_type", "down", "rush", "pass", "qb_scramble",
                          "epa", "success", "yards_gained", "wp", "half_seconds_remaining", "yardline_100",
                          "posteam", "defteam"])
    pb = pb[(pb.season_type == "REG") & pb.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & pb.down.notna() & pb.epa.notna()]
    m = pb.merge(part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"])
    m["season"] = yr
    frames.append(m)
PLAYS = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)
PLAYS = PLAYS[PLAYS.defenders_in_box >= 3]               # a few rows record 0-2: "not recorded"
PLAYS["designed_run"] = (PLAYS.rush == 1) & (PLAYS.qb_scramble != 1)
PLAYS["dropback"] = PLAYS["pass"] == 1

neutral = PLAYS[PLAYS.down.isin([1, 2]) & PLAYS.wp.between(0.2, 0.8) & (PLAYS.half_seconds_remaining > 120)
                & (PLAYS.yardline_100 > 10)].copy()
neutral["box"] = neutral.defenders_in_box.clip(5, 8).astype(int)
neutral["era"] = np.where(neutral.season <= 2022, "2018–2022 (NGS)", "2023–2025 (FTN)")


def mean_ci(d):
    return pd.Series({"epa": d.epa.mean(), "ci": 1.96 * d.epa.std() / np.sqrt(len(d)), "n": len(d)})


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.2), sharey=True)
labels = {5: "5 or\nfewer", 6: "6", 7: "7", 8: "8 or\nmore"}
for ax, (flag, ttl) in zip(axes, [("designed_run", "Designed runs"), ("dropback", "Dropbacks")]):
    for i, (era, g) in enumerate(neutral[neutral[flag]].groupby("era")):
        s = g.groupby("box").apply(mean_ci)
        xs = np.arange(len(s)) + (i - 0.5) * 0.16
        ax.errorbar(xs, s.epa, yerr=s.ci, marker="o", ms=4.5, lw=1.8, capsize=2.5, color=style.SERIES[i],
                    label=era)
    ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
    ax.set_xticks(range(4), [labels[k] for k in range(5, 9)], fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("defenders in the box at the snap", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("EPA per play", fontsize=8)
axes[1].legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read the left panel first. The more defenders in the box, the worse runs do: on these downs, designed runs averaged
about −0.03 EPA against five or fewer in the box, −0.05 against six, −0.09 against seven and −0.15 against eight or
more, and their success rates fell from about 41% to 34% across the same range.[^boxepa] Both data sources agree on
the slope. The plus-one is real: each defender the defense adds to the box takes something away from the run.

Now the right panel, which is the part that explains the two-high era. The same extra defender *helps the passing
game*. Dropbacks against five or fewer in the box averaged about +0.06 EPA; against seven, about +0.12; against eight or
more, about +0.16 in the 2018–2022 data. The box is a budget: a defender spent near the line is a defender not spent in
coverage, and the offense's passing game cashes the difference. (The 2023–2025 point for eight or more dropbacks rests on
only about 800 plays, which is why its interval is so wide.)

And look at the two panels side by side. **Against every box count, the average dropback beats the average designed
run.** Even against the lightest boxes, runs averaged less than zero EPA; even against the heaviest, dropbacks averaged
more than zero. That is the quiet argument for the light box. A defense that keeps two safeties deep and invites the
run is steering the offense toward its less efficient option, and paying for it with a few yards per carry that, on
average, are worth less than the passes it took away.

Three cautions keep this honest.

- **The box count is measured at the snap.** A safety who rotates down after the snap, like the one in @fig-plus-one,
  is counted *out* of the box. Some "six-man boxes" in the data were seven-man fits a second later, which makes light
  boxes look a little better against the run than the fits really were.
- **Boxes are chosen, not assigned at random.** Defenses load the box when they expect a run and empty it when they
  expect a pass, and offenses check into runs against light boxes. Holding the down and the game situation fixed, as this
  chart does, removes the worst of that, but not all of it. [A First Look at
  Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) showed how flat these comparisons look
  when you don't.
- **The data changes source between 2022 and 2023.** Next Gen Stats supplied the box count through 2022, FTN's charters
  from 2023, and they draw the box differently, so read the two lines as two measurements, not one trend.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**Finding the force in tracking data.** The "Watch for it" rule (the outermost defender near the line on each side,
inside the widest receiver, is probably the force) is easy to turn into code. Here it is run on the simulated play in
@fig-fit-chart, exported in Big Data Bowl format (these frames are simulated, BDB-format, not real tracking):

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (find the probable force player on each side at the snap)"
def force_candidates(trk, max_depth=7.0, inside_of_wr=1.0):
    """Outermost defender on each side within `max_depth` yards of the line at the snap, ignoring anyone
    aligned on (or outside) the widest receiver on his side: the probable force player. A pre-snap guess:
    rotation after the snap can change it."""
    snap = trk[trk["frameType"] == "SNAP"]
    ball = snap[snap["side"] == "ball"].iloc[0]
    los, mid = ball["x"], ball["y"]
    rows = []
    for side_name, sgn in (("offense's right", -1), ("offense's left", 1)):   # offense faces +x: right = -y
        off = snap[(snap["side"] == "off") & ((snap["y"] - mid) * sgn > 0)]
        widest = ((off["y"] - mid) * sgn).max()
        dfn = snap[(snap["side"] == "def") & ((snap["y"] - mid) * sgn > 0)].copy()
        dfn["width"] = (dfn["y"] - mid) * sgn
        dfn["depth"] = dfn["x"] - los
        dfn = dfn[(dfn["depth"] <= max_depth) & (dfn["width"] <= widest - inside_of_wr)]
        top = dfn.sort_values("width").iloc[-1]
        rows.append({"side": side_name, "probable force": top["displayName"],
                     "yards outside the ball": round(top["width"], 1), "depth": round(top["depth"], 1)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


fit_play = Play(i_form(), sky_defense(), los=35, to_go=None)
print(force_candidates(fit_play.to_tracking()).to_string(index=False))
```

On the right it finds the strong safety, the force in the fit chart; on the left, with no tight end and a deep corner,
it finds the backside end. With real Big Data Bowl files the same function works on a prepared play (this cell is not
run in the build):

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the same rule on real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_1.csv")
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=2022091100, play_id=55)   # any run play
one["displayName"] = one["displayName"].astype(str)
print(force_candidates(one))
```
:::

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks 2012–2015 (the eighth man)"}
The plus-one's most famous modern home was Pete Carroll's Seattle defense, built on single-high
[Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd). Earl Thomas played the deep middle, alone, and Kam
Chancellor, a strong safety built like a linebacker, played near the line as the eighth man in the box. Seattle led the
NFL in scoring defense four years running, 2012 through 2015.[^seattle] Watch any of their games from those seasons for
one thing: where Chancellor is at the snap. He is the force on runs to his side, the plus-one in the box count, and the
reason offenses that wanted to run on Seattle needed an extra blocker. Then watch what happens to Thomas when the
offense fakes the run: he is the only deep defender, which is the cost of the eighth man.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024 (the light box that held)"}
Vic Fangio's first Eagles defense, in 2024, is the light-box argument at full strength. Through the first two weeks
the *Philadelphia Inquirer* reported six or fewer defenders in the box on 73.5% of snaps, the third-highest rate in the
league, and the run defense looked shaky after the Falcons ran through it in Week 2.[^inq2] Over the full season, by
this book's count, opponents' designed runs met six or fewer in the box about two thirds of the time (the third-highest
rate), and the Eagles allowed the fewest EPA per designed run in the league. Every defense Fangio has run since 2019
(he spent 2022 as a consultant) has been among the five that met runs with six or fewer in the box most
often.[^fangiocalc2] What to watch: the two
safeties at 12–14 yards at the snap, the six-man box, and how often an interior lineman ends up with two blockers on him
and doesn't move. The defense is betting on the front, and in 2024 the bet paid off on the way to a Super Bowl LIX win
over Kansas City, 40–22.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2019 (the box that wasn't loaded enough)"}
The 2019 Ravens rushed for 3,296 yards, breaking an NFL team record that had stood since 1978, and Lamar Jackson ran for
1,206 of them on his way to a unanimous MVP.[^ravens] Box math explains why defenses could not simply load up. On a
designed run with Jackson reading a defender, every box needed one more defender than it appeared to, because the
quarterback counts as a blocker. Defenses met the Ravens' designed runs with seven or more in the box about 65% of the
time, slightly more than they did the rest of the league, and still lost: the Ravens averaged about +0.10 EPA per
designed run against seven-man boxes and about +0.04 against eight or more, where the league averaged −0.10 and −0.13.
Jackson's own designed runs averaged about 7.1 yards.[^ravenscalc] What looks like a normal seven-man box on the
broadcast was, against Baltimore, a light one. Watch any 2019 Ravens game for the defender the quarterback is reading,
and count him out of the box.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024 offense (running at two-high)"}
The same season, on the other side of the ball, the Eagles showed what a good run game does to a light box.
Saquon Barkley ran for 2,005 yards, the ninth 2,000-yard season in NFL history.[^barkley] Against Philadelphia,
defenses played six or fewer in the box on about 61% of designed runs (the league rate was about 59%), and the Eagles
averaged about 5.4 yards per designed run against those boxes, against the league's 4.7. About one in seven of those
runs gained ten yards or more.[^eaglescalc] That is the light box's bill, paid in full: when the front cannot hold six
blockers and the safeties arrive at five yards instead of three, the runs that get past them go a long way. What to
watch: the safeties' depth at the snap, the double teams on the interior, and the moment Barkley reaches the second level
one-on-one with a safety coming downhill.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Before the snap**

- **Count the box, then count the blockers.** Five linemen, plus every tight end and fullback near the line. If the
  quarterback is a runner who reads a defender, add him. More defenders than blockers: the defense has its plus-one in
  the box. Even: the plus-one is a safety, and he will arrive late.
- **Find the force on each side.** Look for the outermost defender within about seven yards of the line and inside the
  widest receiver. A safety walked down outside the tight end: safety force (likely Cover 3). Corners squatting at five
  yards with both safeties deep: corner force (likely Cover 2). Nobody out there but the end: the end is the force.
- **Check the safeties' depth.** At 12–14 yards, they are alley players from depth and the box is what you see. At 8–10
  yards and creeping, one of them is probably coming down at the snap.

**After the snap**

- **Did a safety rotate down?** That is the plus-one arriving.
- **Watch the end man meet the kick-out or the puller.** Dives under it: spill, so look outside for the force. Stays
  square, outside arm free: box, so look inside for the linebacker filling.
- **Did the run bounce?** If it did, who met it outside, the force or nobody? If nobody, rewind and find the empty gap.
- **On a cutback, find the backside linebacker.** If he flowed with everyone else, that is the gap the runner used.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. Who's the force?** First-and-10, 11 personnel. The offense is about to run outside, to its right, toward
the tight end and the Z receiver. Before the snap the defense shows the picture below. Who is the force on the play
side, who is the alley player, and where do you expect the run to end up?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: before the snap. Both safeties are deep, 12 yards off the ball and outside the hashes; both corners are squatting at about 5 yards, a step outside their receivers, facing the quarterback; six defenders in the box against six blockers."
off = single_back_11()
dfn = even4() + [D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 4.5, -15.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 4.5, 15.8, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 10.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -10.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: who forces a run to the right?")
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-8.5, 15.0))
dashed(f, p, [(-7.0, 0.0), (-5.6, 4.0), (-2.6, 8.5), (0.4, 11.0)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4)
say(f, p, -4.6, 11.8, "the run is\nheaded here", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The right cornerback is the force; the strong safety is the alley player.** Two deep safeties and two corners
squatting at five yards, outside their receivers, with their eyes on the quarterback is the classic Cover 2 shape. The corners have no deep zone
to protect, so the play-side corner is free to come up outside-in, keep the ball inside him and turn it back. The
strong safety, starting at twelve yards, reads run and comes down into the alley between the corner and the box.

Expect the run to be turned back inside around the numbers, and expect the defense to *give up some yards* doing it:
six in the box against six blockers is a light box, and the alley player is arriving from twelve yards. The offense's
best counter is a receiver blocking the corner (the Z cracking down, or simply blocking him out), which is why, against
Cover 2, the wide receivers' blocks matter so much in the run game. One caution: corners squatting at five yards can also
be a disguise, bailing to deep thirds at the snap
([Disguise and Rotation](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)). If that happens, the force
becomes whoever rotates down, usually a safety.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. Do the box math.** Second-and-6. The offense is in shotgun with 11 personnel, and its quarterback is one of
the league's most dangerous runners. The defense shows two high safeties and six defenders in the box. How many
blockers does the offense really have, who is the defense's free man, and what run do you expect?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: before the snap. Shotgun, one back beside the quarterback, a tight end on the right; four defensive linemen and two linebackers in the box, a nickel back outside it on the left, two safeties at 12 to 13 yards."
off = single_back_11(gun=True)
dfn = even4() + [D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -6.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.0, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.5, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=6, title="Drill 2: count the box, then count the blockers")
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-8.0, 15.0))
lane(f, p, -5.4, 6.9, -0.6, 7.0, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.05)
say(f, p, 9.2, 0.0, "the box", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Seven blockers against six, and the free men are twelve yards away.** Five linemen and the tight end make six
blockers, and the box holds six defenders: even. But a quarterback who runs and reads counts as a blocker, because the
defender he reads is "blocked" by the read. So on a zone read the offense is effectively seven against six, plus-one *in
the offense's favour*. The defense's free men are the two safeties.

Expect a zone read, or a run with the quarterback as a threat, and expect it to gain four or five yards before a safety
arrives, unless the defense has a plan. Its plans: rotate a safety down at the snap (watch for one creeping toward 8–9
yards before the ball is snapped), or exchange gaps on the read man (the end crashes, a linebacker scrapes to the
quarterback, @fig-exchange). If the safeties stay deep and the end sits still, this is the Ravens' 2019 picture, and
it is a good one for the offense.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. The force is the target.** First-and-10. The offense is in the I-formation and the defense is in a
single-high shell with the strong safety down outside the tight end, the shape of @fig-fit-chart. One thing is
different: the Z receiver has lined up much closer to the formation than usual. What is the offense planning, and who
on the defense has to be ready?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: before the snap. 21 personnel in the I-formation; a 4-3 Over with the strong safety down at about 6 yards outside the tight end and one deep safety. The Z receiver is in a tight split, about 9 yards from the ball instead of out near the numbers."
off = [q.moved(w=9.0) if q.key == "Z" else q for q in i_form()]
dfn = over_front() + [D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS"),
                      D("LCB", "CB", 7.5, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 11.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 3: why is the Z so close?")
p.highlight("Z", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.0, 18.0), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
point_to(f, p, (-4.8, 13.2), (-1.5, 9.0), "tight split", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A crack block on the force, so the cornerback must replace him.** The defense's fit against power depends on the
strong safety: he is the force, the man outside the spill. A receiver in a tight split is in perfect position to block
*down* on him at the snap, a [crack block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-block)
([Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd)), from the side, where
the safety is not looking. If the defense spills the kick-out and the force has been cracked, the bounce has nobody
outside it.

So the defender who must be ready is the right cornerback. His rule is *crack-replace*: when the receiver in front of
him blocks in, he stops thinking about his deep third and comes up to become the force himself. Many defenses also check
out of the spill call when a receiver cracks, boxing the kick-out instead so the ball stays inside. Watch the corner's
first step after the snap. If it is forward and outside, the defense saw the crack coming. If it is backward, the run is
going to the sideline.
:::
:::

## Back to the replay

Return to the opening play. The offense ran power to the right; the end man threw himself under the fullback; the back
bounced outside and was tackled by a safety who started twelve yards deep. Now you can name every piece of it. The end man
was the **spill** player, and the pile he made was the point: the pulling guard had no lane, and the ball went sideways.
The safety who made the tackle was either the **force** (if he had come down to the edge) or the **alley player** (if
he filled the lane inside the force from depth), and he had been free all along, the defense's **plus-one**, never
assigned to any blocker. The analyst said "great fit" because every defender between the ball and the sideline did his
job and nobody did anyone else's. Nobody beat a block. The arithmetic did the work.

## Takeaways

- **A run fit is an eleven-man plan.** Every gap has exactly one owner (gap integrity), and every owner knows how his
  gap moves when the blocking changes. Two defenders in one gap means an empty gap somewhere else.
- **Force turns the ball back inside.** The force defender is a role, not a position: the end, a linebacker, a safety
  or a corner, depending on the call. The coverage usually decides who is free to be him (safety force in Cover 3,
  corner force in Cover 2).
- **Spill and box send the ball to opposite places.** Spill wrong-arms the kick-out and bounces the ball outside to
  speed; box keeps the outside arm free and squeezes the ball inside to the linebackers. Each is a promise about who is
  waiting, and the alley player fills the lane between the box and the force.
- **The plus-one is the extra defender, and it usually comes from a safety.** Offenses erase it with an extra blocker,
  a quarterback read or a pass; defenses get it back with rotation, gap exchanges or two-gapping fronts. Count the
  quarterback when he runs.
- **The light box is a bet, not a mistake.** Two-high defenses give up a few yards per carry to protect against the
  explosive pass. In 2018–2025 data, each extra box defender cost runs about as much as it gave passes, and the average
  dropback beat the average run at every box count.
